state.case_summary:
A 36-year-old man with no prior medical history presented with a 4-year history of diffuse bone pain around the knees and elbows and intermittent generalized pruritus. Over the past 2 months, his bone pain worsened and he developed blurred vision, bilateral exophthalmos, and difficulty walking. Previous workups at multiple centers were nondiagnostic; he had been treated intermittently with analgesics, vitamin D, topical steroids, and antihistamines.

On admission, he appeared well and was hemodynamically stable. Laboratory studies showed:
• White-cell count and differential: normal  
• Hemoglobin: normal  
• Platelet count: mild thrombocytosis (120 × 10^9/L)  
• Renal and liver function tests: normal  
• Tumor markers and autoimmune serologies: negative  
• C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate: mildly elevated  

Radiographic studies demonstrated:
• Knee radiographs: bilateral symmetric sclerotic changes of the distal femora and proximal tibiae  
• Humeral radiographs: intramedullary sclerosis of the distal humeri  
• Forearm radiographs (lateral view): sclerosis of the proximal ulnae and radii without fracture  

Nuclear and cross-sectional imaging revealed:
• 99mTc bone scintigraphy and FDG-PET: bilateral symmetric uptake in long bones, right clavicle, and mandible, with uptake in subcutaneous and muscle tissues of the lower limbs  
• CT and MRI of the lower limbs: multifocal intramedullary sclerosis of the femora and tibiae  
• MRI of the brain: enhancing lesions in the pituitary gland and retrobulbar soft tissues  
• PET/CT of the brain: corresponding FDG-avid lesions  
• CT and PET/CT of the abdomen: bilateral perinephric soft-tissue thickening with FDG uptake  

A CT-guided biopsy of the left proximal tibia showed diffuse infiltration by foamy histiocytes and fibrosis with rare Touton-like giant cells. Immunohistochemical staining of the histiocytes was positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa, and negative for CD1a, S100, and langerin; no granulomas or malignant cells were identified.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Erdheim-Chester disease
B. Langerhans cell histiocytosis was excluded because “the histiocytes were … negative for CD1a … and langerin
C. Rosai
D. Granulomatous disorders (e.g., Wegener’s granulomatosis, neurosarcoidosis) were excluded because there were “no
E. Malignant neoplasia was excluded because the biopsy showed “no … malignant cells” and was “negative for malignancy
F. None
G. None
H. None

bilateral symmetric sclerotic changes on radiographs
multifocal intramedullary sclerosis on CT and MRI

excluded_candidates: Infection: lack of fever, normal white-cell count, and negative autoimmune serologies make this less likely
Malignancy: no malignant cells identified on biopsy, and tumor markers are negative
Autoimmune disorder: negative autoimmune serologies, but some findings could be consistent with an autoimmune process
